steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on distilling Deep Ensemble uncertainty into a single student network for semantic segmentation. Motivate uncertainty quantification for safety-critical segmentation, cover existing methods and knowledge distillation, introduce our approach, and outline the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Semantic segmentation and shortcomings of neural networks
2. Uncertainty quantification methods and their cost; knowledge distillation
3. Our approach
4. Paper outline

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Segmentation
- assign class label to each pixel -> understand semantic content; = pixel-wise classification
- deep neural networks now most popular and successful
- top performance on Cityscapes, PASCAL VOC, but: lack interpretability, can't tell in-domain from out-of-domain, overconfident
- severe for safety-critical apps (autonomous driving, medical imaging) and high-reliability tasks (industrial inspection, automation)

2. Uncertainty quantification
- makes applications safer / more reliable: risk-averse predictions, feedback to human operator when uncertain
- methods: Bayesian Neural Networks, Monte Carlo Dropout, Deep Ensembles
- all need expensive sampling of output distribution from stochastic process
- knowledge distillation recently proposed as solution
- teacher (complex) -> student (smaller); student performance improved

3. Our approach (Deep Uncertainty Distillation using Ensembles for Segmentation, Figure 1)
- student-teacher distillation with Deep Ensembles; approximates predictive uncertainties; simple, adaptable
- single forward pass vs. Deep Ensembles -> much lower inference time, no computational overhead
- simpler than and outperforms previous Deep Ensembles-based uncertainty distillation; evaluated on Cityscapes
- Deep Ensembles replaceable by any other UQ method

4. Outline
- Sec 2 related work (UQ, KD); Sec 3 method; Sec 4 quantitative + qualitative analysis, misclassified pixels, out-of-domain samples on Cityscapes; Sec 5 discussion; Sec 6 conclusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Semantic segmentation is a computer vision task where the aim is to assign a class label to each pixel of an image, with the goal of understanding the semantic content of the image. So it can be seen as a pixel-wise classification task. Recently, methods based on deep neural networks have become the most popular and successful way to solve this problem. They have unrivaled performance on established benchmark datasets like Cityscapes or PASCAL VOC, but neural networks lack interpretability, they cannot distinguish between in-domain and out-of-domain samples, and they tend to be overconfident. These shortcomings are especially severe for safety-critical applications like autonomous driving and the analysis of medical imaging, or for computer vision tasks with high demands on reliability like industrial inspection and automation.

Quantifying the predictive uncertainty is a promising way to make these applications safer and more reliable, for example by making risk-averse predictions preemptively or by giving feedback to a human operator when the predictions are uncertain. Some of the most relevant methods are Bayesian Neural Networks, Monte Carlo Dropout, and Deep Ensembles. Unfortunately, all of these methods need a computationally expensive estimation of a distribution of outputs by sampling from a stochastic process. Recently, the concept of Knowledge Distillation was introduced as a potential solution. Knowledge distillation is a technique to transfer the knowledge in a complex model, called the teacher, to a smaller model, called the student. By incorporating the knowledge learned by the more complex model, the performance of the student can be improved.

- our approach: 'Deep Uncertainty Distillation using Ensembles for Segmentation' (Figure 1)
- student-teacher distillation with Deep Ensembles; approximates predictive uncertainties; simple and adaptable
- single forward pass vs. Deep Ensembles -> much lower inference time, no overhead
- simpler than and outperforms previous Deep Ensembles-based uncertainty distillation; evaluated on Cityscapes
- Deep Ensembles could be swapped for any other UQ method

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Semantic segmentation is a computer vision task where the aim is to assign a class label to each pixel of an image, with the goal of understanding the semantic content of the image. So it can be seen as a pixel-wise classification task. Recently, methods based on deep neural networks have become the most popular and successful way to solve this problem. They have unrivaled performance on established benchmark datasets like Cityscapes or PASCAL VOC, but neural networks lack interpretability, they cannot distinguish between in-domain and out-of-domain samples, and they tend to be overconfident. These shortcomings are especially severe for safety-critical applications like autonomous driving and the analysis of medical imaging, or for computer vision tasks with high demands on reliability like industrial inspection and automation.

Quantifying the predictive uncertainty is a promising way to make these applications safer and more reliable, for example by making risk-averse predictions preemptively or by giving feedback to a human operator when the predictions are uncertain. Some of the most relevant methods are Bayesian Neural Networks, Monte Carlo Dropout, and Deep Ensembles. Unfortunately, all of these methods need a computationally expensive estimation of a distribution of outputs by sampling from a stochastic process. Recently, the concept of Knowledge Distillation was introduced as a potential solution. Knowledge distillation is a technique to transfer the knowledge in a complex model, called the teacher, to a smaller model, called the student. By incorporating the knowledge learned by the more complex model, the performance of the student can be improved.

In this work we present a new approach for efficient and reliable uncertainty quantification, which we call 'Deep Uncertainty Distillation using Ensembles for Segmentation', shown in Figure 1. It applies student-teacher distillation with a Deep Ensembles to accurately approximate predictive uncertainties, while keeping simplicity and adaptability. Compared to the Deep Ensembles, only one forward pass is needed to get predictive uncertainties, which massively reduces the inference time and eliminates the computational overhead. Our method both simplifies and outperforms previous work on Deep Ensembles-based uncertainty distillation, which we evaluate experimentally on the Cityscapes dataset. Also, the Deep Ensembles can in principle be replaced by any other Uncertainty Quantification method.

In Section 2 we give a brief overview of related work on Uncertainty Quantification and Knowledge Distillation, and in Section 3 we describe the methodology of our approach. In Section 4 we show what it can do through quantitative and qualitative analysis of the predictive uncertainties, and the potential to identify wrongly classified pixels and out-of-domain samples on the Cityscapes dataset. Section 5 discusses the experimental results and their potential impact on future research, and Section 6 concludes the paper.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Semantic segmentation is a computer vision task that aims to assign a class label to each pixel in a given image, with the goal of understanding the semantic content of the image. Hence, it can be viewed as a pixel-wise classification task. Recently, methods based on deep neural networks have become the most popular and successful approach to solve this problem [1]. Despite their unrivaled performance on established benchmark datasets like Cityscapes [2] or PASCAL VOC [3], neural networks lack interpretability [4], are unable to distinguish between in-domain and out-of-domain samples [5], and tend to be overconfident [6]. These shortcomings are especially severe for safety-critical applications like autonomous driving [7] and the analysis of medical imaging [8], or for computer vision tasks with high demands on reliability like industrial inspection [9] and automation [10].

Quantifying the predictive uncertainty is a promising way to make such applications safer and more reliable, e.g., by preemptively making risk-averse predictions or by providing feedback to a human operator when predictions are uncertain. Some of the most relevant methods include Bayesian Neural Networks [11], Monte Carlo Dropout [12], and Deep Ensembles [13]. Unfortunately, all of these methods require a computationally expensive estimation of a distribution of outputs by sampling from a stochastic process. Recently, the concept of Knowledge Distillation has been introduced as a potential solution [14,15,16,17]. Knowledge distillation is a technique for transferring the knowledge embodied in a complex model, referred to as the teacher, to a smaller model, referred to as the student. By incorporating the knowledge learned by a more complex model, the student’s performance can be enhanced [18,19,20].

In this work, we present a novel approach for efficient and reliable uncertainty quantification, which we call 'Deep Uncertainty Distillation using Ensembles for Segmentation', as shown in Figure 1. It applies student-teacher distillation with a Deep Ensembles to accurately approximate predictive uncertainties while maintaining simplicity and adaptability. In comparison to the Deep Ensembles, only a single forward pass is required to obtain predictive uncertainties, which massively reduces the inference time and eliminates the computational overhead. Our approach simultaneously simplifies and outperforms previous work on Deep Ensembles-based uncertainty distillation, which we experimentally evaluate on the Cityscapes dataset. Additionally, the Deep Ensembles can in principle be substituted by any other Uncertainty Quantification method.

After a brief overview of related work on Uncertainty Quantification and Knowledge Distillation in Section 2, the methodology of our approach is described in Section 3. In Section 4, we demonstrate its ability through quantitative and qualitative analysis of the predictive uncertainties, and the potential to identify wrongly classified pixels and out-of-domain samples on the Cityscapes dataset. Section 5 discusses the experimental results and their potential impact on future research, while Section 6 concludes the paper.
